title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome: Confirm Median Neuropathy and Protect Function
bottomLine: Carpal tunnel syndrome is median-nerve compression at the wrist diagnosed clinically in a compatible pattern; electrodiagnostics are reserved for uncertainty, severe deficit or procedural planning. Night splinting and cause/risk review are first-line for many patients, while objective weakness or thenar atrophy requires timely surgical assessment.
recognize: Nocturnal numbness/tingling in the thumb-index-middle/radial ring fingers and hand shaking for relief are classic; weakness/thenar wasting indicates more advanced disease.
differentiate: Cervical radiculopathy, proximal median neuropathy and generalized polyneuropathy can mimic CTS.
assessment: Assess sensory distribution, thenar strength/atrophy, provocative wrist maneuvers, occupation/repetitive load, pregnancy, diabetes and thyroid/inflammatory disease when clinically relevant.
workup: Typical mild/moderate CTS can be diagnosed clinically; use nerve-conduction/electrodiagnostic testing for atypical symptoms, persistent weakness, diagnostic uncertainty or preoperative severity assessment when required.
management: Use neutral-position night splinting and ergonomic/load modification; corticosteroid injection can provide selected short-term relief.
Refer persistent function-limiting symptoms, objective weakness/atrophy or severe electrodiagnostic disease for decompression evaluation.
medicationSafety: Repeated steroid injection should not delay decompression when progressive motor deficit is present.
redFlags: Diffuse neurologic deficits inconsistent with CTS
counselling: Teach neutral wrist positioning and that persistent weakness is more concerning than intermittent tingling alone.
followUp: Reassess sensory and motor function after conservative therapy and escalate progression.
examTrap: Ordering electrodiagnostics for every classic mild CTS presentation—or continuing injections despite progressive thenar weakness.
oneLinePearl: CTS becomes urgent when compression starts stealing motor function.

title: Trigger Finger: Stenosing Tendon Sheath Disease, Not Joint Locking
bottomLine: Trigger finger is stenosing flexor tenosynovitis causing painful catching or locking at the A1 pulley. Diagnose clinically, distinguish it from joint disease or tendon rupture, then use activity modification, splinting/injection or hand referral according to severity and persistence.
recognize: Painful clicking/catching with flexion-extension and focal A1-pulley tenderness are typical; diabetes increases risk.
differentiate: MCP arthritis, Dupuytren disease and tendon rupture create different motion abnormalities.
assessment: Assess which digit, duration, fixed locking, palpable nodule/tenderness, diabetes/inflammatory disease and hand function.
workup: Routine imaging is unnecessary for a classic presentation unless trauma or alternate joint pathology is suspected.
management: Use activity modification/splinting and consider corticosteroid injection for persistent symptomatic disease; refer fixed locking, recurrent disease or failed appropriate conservative care for release.
medicationSafety: Injection requires sterile technique and caution with diabetes-related transient hyperglycemia; repeated injections have diminishing benefit/tendon risk.
counselling: Explain that the catching occurs at the tendon pulley rather than because the finger joint is 'out of place'.
followUp: Reassess locking and function after treatment.
examTrap: Imaging a classic trigger finger extensively or mistaking infectious flexor tenosynovitis for routine stenosing disease.
oneLinePearl: Trigger finger is a tendon-pulley problem; infection is the dangerous mimic.

title: Plantar Fasciitis: Load-Related Heel Pain with a Rehabilitation Plan
bottomLine: Plantar fasciitis is usually a clinical diagnosis of plantar-medial heel pain worst with first steps after rest. Treat with load modification, calf/plantar fascia stretching and progressive strengthening; image or broaden the differential when the pattern is atypical or persistent.
recognize: First-step morning pain and focal medial calcaneal tenderness are typical.
differentiate: Calcaneal stress fracture, inflammatory enthesitis, nerve entrapment, fat-pad pain and infection have different clues.
assessment: Assess activity/load change, footwear, BMI/weight-bearing load without stigma, calf tightness, neurologic symptoms, systemic inflammatory features and focal bone tenderness.
workup: No routine imaging is required for a classic presentation; use imaging when stress fracture, mass, inflammatory disease or prolonged atypical course is suspected.
management: Use supportive footwear, stretching and progressive foot/calf strengthening; temporary inserts/taping can support recovery.
Refer persistent refractory disease or alternative structural diagnosis as appropriate.
medicationSafety: Repeated corticosteroid injection can increase fascia rupture/fat-pad risk and is not first-line routine management.
redFlags: Inability to bear weight after sudden load
counselling: Explain that improvement is gradual and depends on consistent load management rather than bed rest.
followUp: Reassess adherence, diagnosis and functional progress if symptoms persist.
examTrap: Ordering an X-ray because a heel spur must be the cause or prescribing prolonged rest instead of progressive rehabilitation.
oneLinePearl: First-step heel pain is usually a load problem treated by progressive loading, not a spur problem.

title: Osteoporosis: Fracture Risk Determines Treatment
bottomLine: Osteoporosis care is fracture-risk care. Use age/risk-appropriate bone density and clinical fracture-risk assessment, recognize that a fragility fracture can establish high risk regardless of T-score, and select anti-fracture therapy with a clear duration/transition plan.
recognize: Prior fragility fracture, glucocorticoids, falls, low BMD and selected secondary causes raise fracture risk.
differentiate: Osteomalacia, hyperparathyroidism and CKD-mineral bone disorder require different treatment; low BMD alone does not identify the cause.
assessment: Assess fracture/fall history, medications, glucocorticoids, nutrition, alcohol/smoking, renal function, menopause/hypogonadism and secondary-cause clues.
workup: Use BMD and fracture-risk tools according to Osteoporosis Canada guidance and targeted labs for secondary causes.
management: Use exercise/falls prevention, adequate calcium/vitamin D intake and risk-appropriate pharmacotherapy.
Choose bisphosphonate, denosumab, anabolic or other therapy according to fracture risk, renal function, contraindications, access and treatment sequence.
medicationSafety: Denosumab should not be stopped without a transition plan because rebound vertebral fracture risk can occur.
Bisphosphonate therapy requires renal/oral administration and rare atypical-femur/jaw risk review.
counselling: Explain that therapy prevents future fracture and requires long-term planning, not just improvement in a density number.
followUp: Reassess adherence, falls/fractures and treatment sequence; repeat BMD when it will inform management.
examTrap: Treating only the T-score while ignoring a recent fragility fracture—or stopping denosumab without follow-on antiresorptive therapy.
oneLinePearl: The outcome that matters is fracture, not the bone-density number alone.

title: Bone Health in Special Populations: Find the Secondary Risk
bottomLine: Bone-health decisions change with glucocorticoids, premature ovarian insufficiency, eating disorders, malabsorption, CKD, transplant, cancer therapy, pregnancy/lactation and young age. Do not apply routine postmenopausal osteoporosis rules without identifying the secondary physiology and reproductive context.
recognize: Fragility fracture or unexpectedly low BMD in a younger patient should trigger secondary-cause evaluation.
Glucocorticoids can raise fracture risk before major BMD loss is obvious.
differentiate: Pregnancy/lactation-associated bone loss, CKD-MBD, osteomalacia and medication-induced bone loss require distinct pathways.
assessment: Review age, menstrual/reproductive history, pregnancy/lactation, nutrition/eating disorder, GI disease, CKD, endocrine disease, glucocorticoids, anticonvulsants, cancer/transplant therapy and prior fractures.
workup: Use risk-specific BMD/labs and specialist evaluation rather than universal screening in every young adult.
management: Treat the cause, optimize weight-bearing/resistance exercise and calcium/vitamin D adequacy, and use pharmacotherapy only when benefits/risks fit the population and reproductive plan.
medicationSafety: Many osteoporosis drugs have pregnancy/fertility implications and long skeletal persistence; discuss reproductive plans before therapy in people who may become pregnant.
redFlags: Recurrent fractures in a young person
counselling: Avoid equating low weight or low BMD with personal failure; explain the medical contributors.
followUp: Monitor the underlying disease/medication exposure and fracture risk longitudinally.
examTrap: Applying routine postmenopausal bisphosphonate logic to a young patient without investigating secondary causes or pregnancy plans.
oneLinePearl: Unexpected bone loss means ask why before choosing the drug.

title: Musculoskeletal Imaging: Choose the Modality for the Question
bottomLine: MSK imaging should answer a defined question. Radiographs evaluate many fractures, alignment and advanced OA; ultrasound assesses selected tendon/effusion problems; MRI is valuable for occult fracture, marrow, soft tissue and internal derangement when results will change care—not as a first reflex for nonspecific pain.
recognize: Incidental degenerative abnormalities are common and may not explain symptoms.
differentiate: A normal radiograph does not exclude occult fracture, early infection or soft-tissue injury when suspicion remains high.
assessment: Localize symptoms clinically, define trauma/red flags and decide what diagnosis or management choice the image must address.
workup: Use validated trauma rules and the lowest-complexity modality that can answer the question; escalate imaging when high-risk disease remains plausible despite a negative initial study.
management: Treat the patient, not incidental findings; correlate every reported abnormality with the clinical syndrome before escalating intervention.
medicationSafety: Contrast MRI/CT considerations depend on indication, renal function and product/protocol; avoid contrast without a management-changing reason.
counselling: Explain why more detailed imaging is not always more useful and may reveal unrelated abnormalities.
followUp: Ensure actionable findings have clear ownership and avoid repeating imaging without a new clinical question.
examTrap: Ordering MRI for uncomplicated mechanical pain before a focused exam or treating an incidental degenerative finding as the diagnosis.
oneLinePearl: The best image is the one that answers the next management question.

title: Joint Injection: Diagnosis, Anatomy, Asepsis, and Aftercare
bottomLine: Joint or periarticular injection is appropriate only after the diagnosis and target are clear, infection has been excluded and risks are reviewed. Steroid injection can reduce selected inflammatory/mechanical symptoms, but it does not replace disease-modifying treatment, rehabilitation or source control.
recognize: Intra-articular injection differs from tendon-sheath/bursal injection; target selection matters for efficacy and complication risk.
differentiate: A hot swollen joint must be evaluated for septic/crystal arthritis before steroid injection.
Tendon rupture or uncontrolled structural instability is not fixed by injection.
assessment: Confirm indication, anatomy, overlying skin/infection, anticoagulation/bleeding context, diabetes, prior injections/allergy and post-procedure support.
workup: Aspirate diagnostically when infection/crystal disease is plausible; ultrasound guidance is useful for selected deep or difficult targets.
management: Use sterile technique, correct target/agent/dose within scope/local standards and provide aftercare/return precautions.
Pair injection with rehabilitation and definitive disease management.
medicationSafety: Steroid can cause transient hyperglycemia and local tissue effects; repeated injections may damage cartilage/tendon depending on site/frequency.
Do not inject through cellulitis or into a suspected infected joint.
counselling: Explain expected short-term flare, delayed steroid onset and infection warning signs.
followUp: Document response and avoid serial injection without reassessing diagnosis/function.
examTrap: Injecting a hot effused joint before excluding septic arthritis.
oneLinePearl: A safe injection starts with a safe diagnosis.

title: Physical Therapy Referral: Prescribe Function, Not Just 'PT'
bottomLine: A high-value PT referral states the diagnosis or working syndrome, red flags already assessed, functional deficits, precautions and goals. Rehabilitation should be coordinated with the patient's actual barriers and progress rather than used as a vague endpoint after imaging.
recognize: Most stable mechanical MSK disorders benefit from active exercise/functional rehabilitation more than prolonged rest.
differentiate: PT is inappropriate as the sole next step for fracture instability, septic joint, progressive neurologic deficit, cauda equina, acute tendon rupture or other conditions needing urgent medical/surgical management.
assessment: Define pain/function, ROM/strength/balance, falls risk, work/sport demands, home environment, access and patient goals.
workup: Complete necessary medical/red-flag evaluation before referral; imaging is not a prerequisite for most uncomplicated mechanical disorders.
management: Refer with specific goals such as gait, strength, range, graded loading, balance, vestibular or return-to-work/sport needs.
Coordinate occupational therapy, orthotics, pain, rheumatology or surgery when the disability requires a broader team.
medicationSafety: Use rehabilitation to reduce unnecessary sedative/opioid reliance; monitor analgesic effects that could mask unsafe loading or falls.
counselling: Set expectations that active practice between visits is part of rehabilitation and goals should be functional and measurable.
followUp: Review progress and revise the diagnosis if function is not improving as expected.
examTrap: Ordering MRI before PT for uncomplicated mechanical pain or sending a red-flag neurologic syndrome to routine rehabilitation first.
oneLinePearl: A PT referral is a functional treatment plan, not a disposal bin for musculoskeletal pain.
